2. Facts relevant for disposal of the Rule are, that the petitioner as pre-emptor submitted a pre-emption case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act being No. 58 of 1998 before the learned Joint District Judge, Rangpur contending, inter alia, that he purchased 31-3/4 decimals of land by as many as 5 kabala deeds from different co-sharers by purchase of the holding of CS Khatian 780 corresponding to RS Khatian No. 608 and CS Khatian No. 966 corresponding to RS Khatian No. 791 of mouza Tajhat, Police Station Kotwali, District-Rangpur. It is his further case that his jama was separated by Mutation Case No. 3106 of 1986-87 by order dated 13-3-1987 and he paid the rent. It is his further case that the preemtee Nos. 2 and 3 being purchaser to the land of plot Nos 748 and 749 transferred 3-2/3 decimals of land from plot No. 748 and 4-1/3 decimals of land from plot No. 749 by a kabala deed dated 13-5-1998 in favour of the pre-emptee opposite party No. 1. No notice of that transfer was served upon him. He claimed himself to be a co-sharer by purchase and as well as the contiguous land holder and had presented the said pre-emption case. 

 10. It appears that the pre-emption case was submitted within limitation and the learned Additional District Judge was wrong to hold that the same was barred by limitation. The transfer deed against which the pre-emption has been submitted was valued at Taka 1,00,000, the pre-emptor has deposited Taka 1,10,000. It is a proper deposit in view of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The learned Additional District Judge upon misconception of law held the said deposit to be not proper. That decision is hereby set aside. 

 12. Paragraph 6 of the pre-emption application bears statements that the pre-emptor has got his jama separated vide Mutation Case No. 3106/86-87. So, he was ceased to be a co-sharer by purchase by that separation of jama. The preemptee No.1 purchased the case land from pre-emptee Nos. 2 and 3 by a kabala deed dated 13-5-1988. From the Exhibit Uma it appears that the vendor of the pre-emptee No. 1 i.e. the pre-emptee Nos. 2 and 3 got the jama of the land under pre-emption separated vide Mutation Case No. 1878/83-84 and by order date 29-2-1984 the jama was separated. Pursuant to the said separation of jama a Khatian No. 1571 was opened and that was marked as Exhibit Uma. In view of the Exhibit-Uma the cosharership of the pre-emptor in the case land under pre-emption has ceased to exist. In view of the above, the pre-emptor was not a co-sharer by purchase. 

 19. As per section 96(5)(b) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the word "contiguous" and "contiguity" in clause (b) of sub-section (5) to be interpreted to mean touching or adjacent and not meaning neighboring. 

 22. Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is a beneficial legislation, intended for the convenience of the co-sharer of a holding of land, for pre-emption of fragmentation of such holding and also for the convenience of the tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred. But, in the instant case, the case plot has already been fragmented and the holding has been separated much earlier to the institution of the case. The doctrine of pre-emption has been introduced only to help mutation and amalgamation of the holding. In the instant case, the same having contiguity has ceased to exist.
